title: Design Proteins with RFD4-Proteina Using Reward-Guided Inference-Time Search | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA, with the University of Washington's Institute for Protein Design, releases RFD4-Proteina, an open model and NIM that jointly generate protein sequence and all-atom structure and spend compute via reward-guided inference-time search. Claimed gains are 3.8x faster generation and 84% less peak memory than RFD3 at 200 residues; the post is mostly a PD-L1 binder tutorial and shows no experimental binding results in the text.

insights.claim: Protein design is framed as a search problem: an 8-residue sequence has over 25 billion combinations and a 100-residue sequence exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe, so success depends on guiding where to look.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Value in AI drug discovery shifts toward search and scoring efficiency, i.e. compute allocation, rather than raw generation.
insights.quote: Protein design is a search problem.
insights.locator: Protein design is a search problem

insights.claim: RFD4-Proteina combines explicit backbone coordinates with latent sequence and atomistic variables and an autoencoder decoder that outputs sequence and all-atom structure together, removing the separate inverse-folding handoff to a model such as ProteinMPNN.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: A single-pass pipeline cuts error compounding between stages and simplifies productization as a microservice.

insights.claim: At 200 residues RFD4-Proteina reportedly delivers 3.8x faster generation and uses 84% less peak reserved memory than RFD3, via residue-level latents, diffusion sampling cut from about 400 steps to 60, and CUDA-accelerated oracles.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Lower memory and step counts expand the design batch size per GPU, improving cost per candidate; benchmark is NVIDIA-reported.
insights.locator: RFD4-Proteina is faster and uses less memory than RFD3

insights.claim: The BioIR backend speeds RFD4-Proteina by 1.37 to 1.73x over the default compiled backend across six Hopper GPU configurations; on H100 PCIe suite time drops from 161 to 111 seconds, about 31%.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Software-stack optimization on existing Hopper hardware extends the life of installed GPU fleets for bio workloads.
insights.locator: For faster design iteration, the BioIR backend

insights.claim: The model and kernels were co-designed with the cuEquivariance and BioNeMo Inference Runtime teams, tying the model's performance to NVIDIA's libraries.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Performance advantages rely on NVIDIA-specific kernels, reinforcing CUDA lock-in in computational biology.
insights.locator: The model and kernels were co-designed

insights.claim: During inference-time search the model denoises trajectories, scores partial designs with rewards (geometry, interactions, independent prediction confidence), retains and branches promising states, and continues until criteria are met.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Mirrors test-time compute scaling from LLMs, applied to molecular design; extra compute can be traded for higher-quality candidates.

insights.claim: The example search preset uses two branches, beam width three, scoring at steps 20, 40, 50 and 60, with OpenFold3 pLDDT reward floor of 50 and saves rollouts at reward 80.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Concrete thresholds are tutorial defaults, not tuned results; compute comparisons must include refolding and scoring cost.

insights.claim: The post warns the pLDDT reward measures confidence in the designed binder rather than evidence of binding, so interface and refolding metrics (ipTM, ipSAE, RMSD, TMol interaction energies) must be checked separately.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Optimizing a proxy reward risks Goodhart-style overfitting to predictor confidence; wet-lab validation remains the true filter.
insights.quote: This measures confidence in the binder, not evidence of binding

insights.claim: Search outputs vary in count, and the post advises inspecting generated CIFs and retained metrics before selecting candidates, and including refolding and scoring in compute comparisons.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Cost per validated hit, not per generated structure, is the right unit of comparison for vendors.

insights.claim: RFD4-Proteina is offered as an open model for training and method development and as a NIM microservice with an HTTP interface, with the build.nvidia.com hosted endpoint not recommended for production.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Open weights plus a packaged microservice follows NVIDIA's playbook of seeding research and monetizing deployment on its software stack.
insights.locator: You can access RFD4-Proteina in two ways

insights.claim: The tutorial targets PD-L1, an oncology target (PDB 5O45), designing 100-150-residue binders with hotspots at Tyr56, Met115 and Tyr123, and the model repository was still private at time of writing.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Immuno-oncology binders are a commercially relevant use case, but private repo status limits immediate adoption.

insights.claim: An agent can coordinate generation, search and evaluation via rfd4-proteina-campaign and rfd4-proteina-package skills, while scientists define objectives and use experimental evidence to guide each round.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Agentic design-test loops make lab throughput, not compute, the bottleneck, favoring companies with fast wet-lab cycles.
insights.locator: Run a campaign with an AI agent

insights.claim: The post asserts that, per an accompanying manuscript, RFD4-Proteina is state-of-the-art across a broad set of molecular tasks in quality and throughput, but the post itself gives no experimental validation numbers.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Claims of breadth and state-of-the-art are unverified in this text; treat as vendor assertion pending the manuscript and independent replication.
